t:
(a) In General.—In order to ensure physical security at Federal Aviation Administration staffed facilities that house air traffic control systems, the Administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration shall act immediately to—

        (1) correct physical security weaknesses at air traffic control facilities so the facilities can be granted physical security accreditation not later than April 30, 2004; and 
        (2) ensure that follow-up inspections are conducted, deficiencies are promptly corrected, and accreditation is kept current for all air traffic control facilities.  
    (b) Reports.—Not later than April 30, 2001, and annually thereafter through April 30, 2004, the Administrator shall transmit to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate and the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives a report on the progress being made in improving the physical security of air traffic control facilities, including the percentage of such facilities that have been granted physical security accreditation.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the reporting requirement is a form of consultation, but the reports go only to congressional committees, which are inside the federal government. The rest of the section directs the FAA Administrator to fix security weaknesses and maintain accreditation internally. No outside party such as states, the public, experts, or industry is consulted or given a role in any federal decision.
fable.s: the Administrator shall transmit to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate and the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives a report

opus.w: The only formal interaction in this section is a report from the FAA Administrator to congressional committees, and Congress is inside the federal government. The rest of the section directs the agency to fix security weaknesses and keep accreditation current, with no consultation, hearing, comment period, advisory body or right to sue involving anyone outside the government. Reading the reporting requirement as participation would wrongly treat communication within the government as outside involvement.
opus.s: the Administrator shall transmit to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate and the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives a report on the progress being made in improving the physical security of air traffic control facilities
opus.b:
1. **Thinking it through:** The tempting reading is that the annual "Reports" in subsection (b) are a formal procedure that counts as participation. That fails because the reports go only to Senate and House committees, and Congress is inside the federal government. The rest of the section tells the FAA Administrator to fix physical security weaknesses at air traffic control facilities, which is purely internal. No state, company, expert or member of the public takes part in any decision.

2. **Label:**

qwen_chat.w: The section requires the Administrator to submit reports to congressional committees. Congress is part of the federal government, so reporting to it does not constitute participation by outside parties. The other requirements involve internal agency actions (correcting weaknesses, conducting inspections) without any mandate to consult with or coordinate with non-federal entities.
qwen_chat.s: the Administrator shall transmit to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate and the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives a report on the progress being made in improving the physical security of air traffic control facilities
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that "follow-up inspections" or the general regulatory context implies public participation, but the text only mandates internal agency actions and reporting to Congress. Congress is inside the federal government, so reporting to it is not participation. There is no mention of consulting with the public, states, or other outside entities.
